stack/recap: Take f of u and v is u squared plus two v squared, a bowl, at the point one, one. Its partial derivatives there are partial f, partial u is two and partial f, partial v is four.
stack/grad: Stack the partials into a vector, and you have the gradient of f. It is written nabla f, read “nabla f” after the upside-down triangle, called nabla. Here the gradient of f is two, four.
stack/up: The gradient points the way f climbs fastest: straight up the bowl, across the rings.
stack/down: To make f smaller, step the other way, against the gradient: along minus nabla f.
stack/small: A small step, a tenth of the gradient, lands on a lower ring: f drops from three to one point three six.
shape/loss: A function can take a whole grid of numbers as its input. Here W has three rows and four columns, twelve numbers in all, and f turns them into a single number.
shape/g: So the gradient nabla f has twelve partials, one per entry of W, laid out exactly like W: three by four. Since it holds the slopes of f in the entries of W, it is also written partial f, partial W.
shape/entry: Each entry says how f moves when that one number in W is nudged: the gradient at row one, column two belongs to W at row one, column two.
worked/p: Try one. f of u and v is two u squared, plus u v, plus four v. What is nabla f at one, two?
worked/du: In u, with v held: two u squared gives four u, u v gives v, and four v gives zero. Four plus two is six.
worked/dv: In v, with u held: two u squared gives zero, u v gives u, and four v gives four. One plus four is five. So nabla f is six, five.
